analysis.one_liner: Requires federal safety standards to prevent deadly combustible dust explosions in factories.
analysis.headline: The bill never left a House subcommittee and died without ever coming to a vote, despite following an explosion that killed 14 sugar plant workers.
analysis.plain_summary: After a 2008 sugar refinery explosion killed 14 workers, this bill would have required the Labor Department to quickly issue mandatory workplace rules covering combustible dust — fine particles like sugar, wood, or metal dust that can ignite and explode. It would have mandated hazard assessments, dust cleanup programs, engineering controls, and annual worker training, and made dust a formally recognized workplace hazard. It never received a committee vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in the roughly two dozen industries covered by the bill — food and sugar processing, wood products, plastics, pharmaceuticals, metals, textiles, and others — where dust buildup can turn a spark into a deadly explosion. The bill cites 281 dust incidents between 1980 and 2005 that killed 119 workers and injured 718 [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires an interim federal standard within 90 days, covering hazard assessment, written dust-control programs, engineering controls, and housekeeping rules to prevent dust buildup on floors, ledges, and equipment [S2] [S3].
Requires employers to give workers annual safety training and a voice in hazard assessments, and to revise hazard communication rules so workers are told when dust is explosive [S2] [S3].

The bill's findings describe a quarter of dust explosions occurring at food industry facilities, and note that a 1987 grain dust standard proved highly effective — a model this bill would extend to other industries [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers that handle combustible dust — food, sugar, wood, plastics, chemicals, metals — would pay for inspections, dust collection systems, housekeeping, and building safeguards like explosion venting.

drawbacks.text: The interim standard would take effect within 30 days and skip the usual rulemaking process, including public comment and small-business review, giving employers little time or say before compliance obligations bite [S3].
Compliance costs fall especially on smaller plants; the bill exempted the final standard from small-business procedure but not the interim rule [S3].
A good-faith objection: NFPA dust standards are already voluntary, and some operators argue standards should be tailored industry-by-industry rather than imposed broadly and quickly [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety case is strong: the bill builds on an existing grain-dust standard that OSHA itself found effective, and follows a federal board's finding of 281 incidents, 119 deaths, and 718 injuries [S3]. The main cost is real but conventional — safety retrofits and housekeeping at dust-handling plants — and the biggest design flaw is the fast-tracked interim rule with no public comment or small-business review. On balance, the protections for workers outweigh the costs, though the hurried timeline was a legitimate complaint.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and Labor Committee and then to its Workforce Protections subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended — no hearing, no vote, no floor action.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 4, 2009, days after the first anniversary of the Imperial Sugar refinery explosion in Georgia that killed 14 workers and injured more than 60 [S2] [S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the day it was introduced [S1] [S5].
On March 23, 2009, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections — the last recorded action on the bill [S5].
The bill never received a committee vote or floor vote in the House, and the Senate never considered it before the 111th Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers that handle combustible dust — food, sugar, wood, and chemical processors — avoided mandatory safety retrofits, dust controls, and training costs, and remained subject only to voluntary standards.

for.name: Rep. George Miller
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-CA), bill sponsor and chairman of the Education and Labor Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring OSHA to issue interim and final combustible dust standards.

for.name: Rep. John Barrow
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, representing the district where the Imperial Sugar explosion occurred.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by the bill's own sponsor
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Workforce Protections subcommittee on March 23, 2009, and never reported it out — no markup or vote.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican supported it; the bill never got far enough for a roll call that would show the full partisan split.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed dust hazard assessments, housekeeping rules, and engineering controls on plants like the Imperial Sugar refinery where 14 workers died; a quarter of dust explosions occur at food facilities [S3]. Compliance costs would fall on these plants, but the safety benefit goes to their workers.

industries.industry: Wood products, plastics, and chemical manufacturing
industries.note: Explicitly covered industries that would bear the cost of dust collection systems, building safeguards, and training; without the bill, NFPA dust standards remained voluntary [S3].
Covered by the interim and final standards, including requirements for explosion venting, building design, and hazard segregation [S2] [S3].
